title.en: Blind Elder Cakkhupala and the Wheel of Deeds
title.zh: 失明長老遮拘波羅與業輪

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: At Savatthi the elder Cakkhupala vows to spend the rains without lying down, loses his eyes through his vow, and wins arahatship in the same moment his sight perishes. When visiting monks report that he trampled insects while walking, the Buddha clears him, for the blind arahant cannot see, and tells how a physician in a past life deliberately blinded a woman who cheated him: that deed ripened as blindness through every existence.
summary.zh: 舍衛城的遮拘波羅長老發願結夏安居不躺臥，為守願而失明，於失明同時證得阿羅漢果。外來比丘舉報他踐踏蟲蟻，佛陀為其開脫，並說過去世他為醫者時故意弄瞎賴帳的婦人，此業感果，生生世世失明。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Mahā Pāla, son of a rich merchant of Savatthi, heard the Buddha preach at Jetavana and left his wealth and his grieving brother to become a monk. Asked how he would spend the rains, he resolved to remain upright in three postures and never stretch out his back. In the first month his eyes began to stream with tears. When a villager's physician sent ointment and later questioned him, the elder stayed silent, refusing to lie down even to apply medicine. Confronting himself in verse, he chose the Buddha's teaching over his eyes: let the eyes perish, only the Law must be kept. Given up by the physician as incurable, he resumed his meditations; at the end of the middle watch his eyes and his corruptions were extinguished together, and he became a blind arahant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the rainy season ended, his sixty companion monks went on to see the Teacher, and a novice was sent back to guide the blind elder. On the road the novice heard a woman singing in the forest, released the staff, and sinned with her. The elder, who knew through his own power, refused to let a sinner hold his staff; the shamed novice fled into the forest. The elder resolved to die where he stood. But the stirring of his virtue made Sakka's jeweled throne hot, and Sakka came disguised as a traveler, took the staff's tip, and shortened the road so that the two arrived at Savatthi by evening. The elder's brother received him with weeping and freed two slaves to serve him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: One stormy night the elder walked in the cloister, and insects emerging from the wet earth perished beneath his feet. Visiting monks, seeing the crushed insects, accused him of killing living beings, and the Buddha answered that they had not seen him kill, and that one freed from corruption has no thought of killing. Asked why one destined for arahatship had become blind, the Buddha told a past life: a physician at Benares cured a poor woman's eyes on the promise of her slavery; when she denied her promise he applied an ointment that put her eyes out like a lamp's flame. That physician was Cakkhupala, and for that deed, done with corrupt thought, suffering followed him through every existence, even as a wheel follows the hoof of the ox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 1 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Mattakundali, the Boy Who Answered the Weeping Father
title.zh: 馬塔昆達利與哭月的婆羅門

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A miser named Adinnapubbaka refused to hire a physician for his dying son, Mattakundali, and laid the boy outside to hide his wealth from visitors. With his last strength the boy saw the Buddha in a ray of light and died believing, reborn a god in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Disguised as his own mortal self he met his father at the burning-ground, asked for the sun and moon as wheels for a golden chariot, and shamed him out of weeping for the dead; the father took refuge and hosted the Buddha.
summary.zh: 慳吝的婆羅門阿丁那布巴卡不肯為病重之子馬塔昆達利請醫，怕花費家財，竟將少年抬到屋外。少年見佛光而歸依，命終生三十三天為天神，化形還鄉，向哭屍場的父親索日月為金車輪，點醒他莫為已死者哭泣，並引父親供養佛陀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: The Brahman Adinnapubbaka, called Never-Gave because he gave nothing to anyone, hammered out a pair of golden earrings himself rather than pay a smith's fee, and his son was named Mattakundali, Burnished Earrings. At sixteen the boy fell gravely ill; his father would not summon a physician for fear of wasting his substance, and doctored him with tree-barks until he was past help. At last the Brahman, thinking that all who came to see the dying boy would see his wealth, carried him out and laid him on the terrace. That dawn the Buddha, rising from a trance of compassion, looked over the worlds and saw the boy lying there; he knew the boy would die believing and be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. When he passed by with the monks, he sent a ray of light, and Mattakundali, turning, beheld him. Too weak to move, he fixed his mind on the Teacher and died with a believing heart, and as if awaking from sleep found himself in a golden mansion in the World of the Gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Brahman burned the body and went every day to the burning-ground, weeping, 'Where are you, my only son?' The deity, surveying his glory, saw that his father grieved for what could not be seen, and determined to change his mind. Taking his own mortal form, the youth stood near the burning-ground, wringing his hands. Asked why he wept, he answered that he had a chariot of solid gold but could not find wheels, and when the Brahman promised wheels of gold or jewels, demanded the moon and the sun as brothers twain. The Brahman called him a simpleton crying for the moon; the youth retorted that they who weep for the dead weep for what cannot be seen, and so are the greater fools. Freed from sorrow, the Brahman took refuge in Buddha, Law, and Order, kept the five precepts, and invited the Teacher to a meal. When he asked before the multitude whether faith alone had raised anyone to heaven, the Buddha summoned Mattakundali in his celestial glory, three-quarters of a league tall, and the deity declared before all that he had won heaven solely by beholding and believing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Obstinate Elder Tissa and the Curse at the Potter's Hall
title.zh: 頑固的肥胖帝沙長老與陶師堂詛咒

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Elder Tissa, an old and fat kinsman of the Buddha, refused the courtesies due visiting monks and then refused to ask their pardon even at the Buddha's own instruction. The Buddha told how, as the ascetic Devala, Tissa had once lain across a doorway, cursed his innocent fellow ascetic Narada for treading on him, and would not apologize until the sun itself stood still; even then he begged pardon only when forced. Whoever cherishes 'he abused me' keeps hatred alive forever.
summary.zh: 肥胖老邁的帝沙長老是佛陀親戚，卻怠慢參訪比丘，被勸道歉仍不肯。佛陀說過去他為仙人提瓦羅，橫臥門口，被那羅達仙人無意踩踏即出言詛咒，太陽為此不升，他仍不認錯，最後被國王強壓才道歉。懷恨者不得息恨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Elder Tissa, son of the Buddha's father's sister, was an old man when he left the world and was so fat that visiting monks took him for a great elder and offered to rub his feet. He sat silent in the center of the Hall of State. A young monk snapped his fingers and rebuked him, and Tissa, stung in his warrior's pride, went to the Buddha weeping that the monks abused him. The Teacher went through every courtesy Tissa had failed to perform, and bade him apologize; three times Tissa refused, saying 'They abused me.' The Buddha told the monks that this was not the first time he had been obstinate, and told of a former existence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Long ago at Benares the ascetic Devala shared a potter's hall with the ascetic Narada. At bedtime Devala lay down deliberately across the doorway, so that Narada trod on his matted locks; going out and returning, Narada trod him again. Though Narada begged pardon, Devala cursed him: when the sun rose, may your head split into seven pieces. Narada, who could survey eighty cycles, saw the curse would fall back on his own brother-ascetic, and out of pity held the sun from rising. The citizens wailed to the king, who found the two ascetics at the potter's hall. Only an apology could save Devala, but he refused; the king seized him by hands, feet, and neck and bowed him before Narada, then set him in a lake with a lump of clay on his head. As the sun's rays struck the clay it split in seven pieces, and Devala ducked under the water and fled. At that time, said the Buddha, the king was Ananda, Devala was Tissa, and Narada was the Buddha himself: 'He abused me, he struck me' held in the heart never lets hatred cease.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Barren Wife, the Ogress, and Hatred Quenched by Love
title.zh: 不孕婦與羅剎——恨以愛止

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A barren wife gave her rival abortifacients, and the fruitful wife, dying in childbirth, wished rebirth as a devourer. Through cat, hen, leopardess, and doe each devoured the other's young until one became an ogress who ate two of her rival's newborn sons. When the ogress rushed to seize the third child, the Buddha summoned her, taught that hatred is quenched by love and not by hatred, and converted her; the mother then lodged and fed her, and her weather forecasts made the household prosper.
summary.zh: 不孕妻屢次讓妝妹墮胎，臨產的妝妹發願復仇，歷經貓、母雞、豹、母鹿生生相食，終成羅剎，兩度吞食仇人之子。第三胎時羅剎趕至寺中奪子，佛陀召她前來，教以恨不能以恨止、唯愛能止，度她歸信，並令產婦收留供養，從此家和興旺。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: A wife chosen for a young man proved barren, and fearing she would be displaced, she herself fetched a second bride and then, pretending friendship, gave her abortifacient drugs with each daily porridge until the rival miscarried twice. Warned, the third time the fruitful wife said nothing; but the jealous wife drugged her again when the child was near maturity, and the babe lodged across the womb's mouth. In agony the fruitful wife cried that her three children were dead and wished to be reborn as an ogress able to devour her rival's children; she died and was reborn as a cat in that very house, while the barren wife, beaten in her turn, died and was reborn as a hen. The cat ate the hen's eggs thrice; reborn a leopardess, she ate the doe's young; the doe, reborn an ogress, disguised as a friend entered the young woman's house twice and devoured her new-born sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the young wife was great with child a third time she fled to her parents' home, but the ogress, released from her turn of drawing water at Lake Anotatta, dashed after her. On the naming day, mother and father walked back through the monastery grounds, and the ogress came upon them at the pool. The mother shrieked and dashed into the assembly, laid her boy at the Buddha's feet, and begged her son's life. The Teacher had Ananda summon the ogress, who stood before him, and asked her: had she not come face to face with a Buddha, she and this woman might have cherished hatred for an aeon. 'Hatred is quenched by love, not by hatred. This is an eternal law.' At the stanza's end the ogress was established in stream-entry; the mother, reassured, gave her the child, and the ogress kissed and caressed him and gave him back, weeping only that she had no way to live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Teacher bade the mother take the ogress home and feed her with the choicest rice-porridge. Frightened first by the threshing flail, then by slops, dogs, and boys at every shed, the ogress was lodged at last in a quiet place outside the village, and the porridge was carried daily to her. In return she foretold which fields would drown and which would thirst, and her friend's crops flourished while the neighbors' failed. Asked the secret, the young wife told the whole city to carry choice food to the ogress and she would look after their crops too; all the residents honored her, and from that time the ogress watched over everyone's harvest. Thus, where wrath had promised only devouring, love turned the same creature into a guardian of the fields.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Quarrelsome Monks of Kosambi and the Elephant's Service
title.zh: 憍賞彌諍僧與象王侍佛

region.zh: 憍賞彌喬賞彌精舍、波黎耶迦林

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A dispute over whether a spilt vessel of water was a sin split the monks of Kosambi into factions that spread through the whole world of gods. Three times the Buddha tried to reconcile them and, failing, withdrew alone to Parileyyaka forest, where an elephant swept for him and a monkey offered honey, both reborn as gods. Only when the townsfolk starved the disputants into shame did they beg pardon at Jetavana.
summary.zh: 憍賞彌僧團因潑水是否成罪而起諍，黨派之爭蔓延至梵天。佛陀三度勸和無效，獨往波黎耶迦林過夏；護象掃地供侍，獼猴供蜜，皆生天為神。僧眾受信施冷落而愧悔，至舍衛城求懺，紛爭方息。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: At Kosambi two monks, one a student of the Discipline and one a preacher of the Law, quarreled over a vessel of water left in the bathroom after washing. Each side branded the other a liar, sentence of excommunication was passed, and the lay supporters, the nuns, and at last the deities from the realm of the Four Great Kings to the Heaven of the Gods Sublime all formed two factions. The Buddha sent word twice, 'Let them be united,' and on the third time went to them himself, pointing out the wrong on both sides; then he told them the Jataka of Prince Dighavu, who spared the very king who had killed his father. But they paid no heed, so the Teacher left without a farewell and went alone to the Protected Forest near Parileyyaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: A noble elephant, crowded by his herd, left the forest's wilds and came to serve the Teacher: he swept the ground with a branch, brought water he heated himself with fire-drill and hot stones, carried bowl and robe, fanned him, and paced all night with a club against beasts of prey. A monkey, seeing the elephant's zeal, brought honey in a leaf; finding insect eggs in it, he picked them out gently and offered it again, then leaped with joy from branch to branch until he fell on a stump and died, and for his faith was reborn in the World of the Thirty-three. When Ananda later brought five hundred monks to the forest, the elephant laid down his staff at the Buddha's word; and when at last the Teacher departed for good, telling him he could win no further fruit in this life, the elephant thrust his trunk into his mouth and went off weeping, and died of a broken heart, reborn as the god Parileyyaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Kosambi the townsfolk stopped all civility to the disputing monks: no seats, no salutations, hardly food. Nearly famished within days, they confessed to one another, reconciled, and asked their supporters' pardon, but the rainy season kept them from the Teacher. When at last they came to Savatthi to beg his pardon, the king of Kosala and Anathapindika at first refused to admit them, until the Buddha pleaded their cause. Lodged apart, pointed at wherever they went, 'There they are! There they are!', the monks hung their heads for shame and threw themselves at the Teacher's feet. Only he who remembers no grievance, said the Buddha, ends his hatred, and the assembled monks were established in the Fruit of Conversion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Elder Maha Kala and the Burning-Ground Practice

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Two caravan-brothers became monks with opposite motives. Maha Kala practiced the austere burning-ground discipline, meditating on a beautiful corpse as the fire licked it black, and won arahatship; Culla Kala kept thinking of his wives, was stripped and mocked by them, and returned to the world. When Maha Kala's eight wives tried to drag him back, he rose into the air; the Buddha compared him to a rock-mountain that no wind of Mara can shake.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟商人先後出家：大迦羅在塚間修不淨觀，觀火中屍身而證阿羅漢；小迦羅繫念妻室，被妻子剝衣羞辱，還俗。八位前妻企圖拉大迦羅還俗，他騰空示現。佛陀以堅石之山喻其心不可撼動。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Culla Kala, Majjhima Kala, and Maha Kala, three brothers of Setavya, were on the road to Savatthi with five hundred carts when Maha Kala followed the garland-bearing crowds to hear the Buddha and asked at once to be received into the Order; Culla Kala became a monk only to bring his brother home again. Maha Kala, too old for study, took the Discipline of the Burning-Grounder: by night he went alone to the burning-ground, by dawn returned, and kept the keeper Kali's rules, shunning fish, flesh, oil, and sleep. When a young woman of station died suddenly, Kali showed him the corpse as a subject of meditation; he watched the beautiful golden body blacken as the flames took hold, understood that a body which just now made men forget the Sacred Word had just now attained decay and death, and won arahatship on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Culla Kala's wives, hoping to recover their husband when the Buddha visited, mocked the young monk and stripped his robes; he put on white garments and left the Order the same day. The next day Maha Kala's eight wives laid a similar plot, and after the meal begged him to pronounce the thanksgiving and stay behind. The monks worried what eight wives could do to him; the Teacher answered that Culla Kala lived looking for pleasure, while Maha Kala lived not looking for pleasure, immovable as a mountain of solid rock, and spoke the stanza of the wind that flattens a weak tree but cannot shake a mountain of rock. When his former wives crowded round to tear off his yellow robe, the elder rose from his seat, split the pagoda's peak, and soared through the air, descending only to honor the Teacher's feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: How Sariputta and Moggallana Became the Chief Disciples
title.zh: 舍利弗與目犍連成為上首弟子

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The two friends Upatissa and Kolita, weary of the Mountain-top festival's vanity, left the teacher Sanjaya and found the Deathless through a single line of the Elder Assaji; at Veluvana the Buddha ordained them with 'Come, monks!' Monks grumbled that the latest arrivals were made chief disciples, but the Buddha showed the wishes each had made at former Buddhas' feet: Sarada's flower-parasol held for seven days, and Sirivaddha's offerings, earned them the stations of Sariputta and Moggallana.
summary.zh: 鄔波提沙與拘利陀二友於山頂節會厭倦無常，離開散若耶外道，因阿說示尊者一句「諸法因生」而證初果，至竹林精舍受「善來比丘」出家。眾僧不平，佛陀則述二人過去於阿那瑪達答佛前發願、執蓋供佛七日，方得今日上首弟子之位。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: At the Mountain-top festival in Rajagaha, the two Brahman youths Upatissa and Kolita of villages seven generations in friendship, watched the jests, tears, and almsgiving of the crowds and asked themselves why they should watch people who in a hundred years would all be gone. They renounced the world under the wandering ascetic Sanjaya, soon exhausted his teaching, and made a pact: whichever first attained the Deathless would tell the other. In Rajagaha Upatissa saw the monk Assaji going his alms-round with calm senses, and when told that the Buddha was his teacher, begged the substance only; the single line, 'Of all things that proceed from a cause, the Tathagata has told the cause,' established Upatissa in stream-entry, and the same stanza won Kolita. They went to Sanjaya, who refused to become a pupil again, 'as absurd as for a chatty to go to the well,' and with two hundred and fifty followers they came to Veluvana, where the Teacher, seeing them from afar, told the monks these two would be his chief and noble pair, and ordained them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: On that same evening the Buddha assigned them the places of Chief Disciples, and the senior monks protested that the Band of Five, Yasa's fifty-four, the Thirty Youths, and the three Kassapa brothers all deserved the honor first. The Buddha answered that he gave only what each had wished for at former Buddhas' feet. Ajjina-Kondanna had given the first-fruits of one crop nine times under the Buddha Vipassi, wishing only to be first to win arahatship; the three brothers Kassapa had fed the Congregation while their steward and treasurer ate what was meant for the monks, and were reborn as ghosts until King Bimbisara, their former steward and treasurer, transferred his alms-merit to them; but Sariputta, then the ascetic Sarada, had wished for the place of Chief Disciple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: An incalculable ago, Sarada was a learned anchorite with seventy-four thousand matted-locks followers. When the Buddha Anomadassi descended from the sky before him, Sarada recognized the marks of a Buddha, held a flower-parasol over him for seven days while his pupils spread a bed of flowers a league long, and refused celestial sovereignty to wish instead for the station of this Buddha's Chief Disciple. His friend Sirivaddha, won at last, gave alms for seven days and wished for Second Disciple; the Buddha prophesied both wishes would ripen in the dispensation of Gotama. The Teacher then rebuked Sanjaya's disciples for finding truth in falsehood and falsehood in truth, and spoke the pair of stanzas on those who attain the goal of truth and dwell in right thinking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Nanda Won by the Celestial Nymphs

region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城、舍衛城祇園精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: On his wedding day Prince Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, was led away by the returning of his alms-bowl and ordained against his will, longing for his bride Janapada-Kalyani. The Buddha flew him to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, showed him five hundred pink-footed nymphs beside whom his wife was like a scalded monkey, and guaranteed him their prize; mocked as a hireling, Nanda strove and won arahatship, releasing the Teacher from his promise.
summary.zh: 難陀王子成婚之日被佛陀以缽引至僧團，不情願出家，仍思念未婚妻佳夷雅妮。佛陀攜他上三十三天，見五百位粉足天女，其妻如斷耳斷尾的燒傷獼猴。難陀為天女勤修，被譏為「僱工」，終證阿羅漢，佛陀亦解其諾言。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: When the Buddha visited Kapilavatthu, the ceremonies of Prince Nanda's sprinkling, house-warming, and marriage were in progress. The Teacher entered for alms, placed his bowl in Nanda's hands, and departed without taking it; out of reverence Nanda dared not say 'Receive your bowl,' but followed, thinking the bowl would be taken at the head of the stairs, at the foot, in the court. Word came that his bride Belle-of-the-Country, Janapada-Kalyani, half-combed and streaming tears, was running after them; she begged him to return, but the Teacher led him to the monastery and asked whether he wished to be a monk. Reverence overcame him, he said yes, and was ordained. Days later he told the brethren he could not endure the religious life, for he kept remembering his wife's words, 'Please return immediately.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Teacher took Nanda by the arm and flew him to the World of the Thirty-three, showing him on the way a scorched monkey on a burnt stump, its ears, nose, and tail consumed by fire; then five hundred pink-footed celestial nymphs waiting on Sakka. Asked which was fairer, Nanda judged his wife as far below the nymphs as the maimed monkey below her. 'Cheer up, Nanda; I guarantee you these five hundred nymphs.' The monks, hearing of the bargain, treated him as a hireling bought with a price, and the mockery stung him to strive; living secluded, heedful, and ardent, he soon won arahatship. A deity came by night to report it, and Nanda himself released the Teacher from his promise, since the Teacher had read his mind and seen when his heart was freed. The Buddha compared him to a house now well thatched, which lust as rain can no longer break through, and told of the merchant Kappata, whose balky donkey was led home only by the lure of a promised mate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Cunda the Pork-Butcher Sees Hell While Still Alive

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: For fifty-five years Cunda killed pigs by pouring boiling water down their throats, yet the Buddha lived at a neighboring monastery all that time without his ever offering so much as a handful of flowers. When a malady struck him, the fire of Avici hell rose before his eyes while he still lived: for seven days he crawled about his barricaded house grunting and squealing like a pig, then died into the Great Hell itself.
summary.zh: 豬屠錢達五十五年以沸水灌豬喉宰豬營生，佛陀近在鄰寺他卻從未供養過一捧花。病發之時，阿鼻地獄之火生前現前，他被家人鎖在屋內，學豬叫爬行七日而死，墮入阿鼻地獄。作惡者今生與來世兩處受苦。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Cunda the pork-butcher made his living for fifty-five years by killing pigs. In famine he carted rice to the villages and brought back shoats bought for a pint-pot or two of rice apiece; in the pen behind his house he fed them on shrubs and excrement, and when he slaughtered one he clubbed it, forced a wedge into its jaws, poured boiling water down its throat until the belly ran clean, peeled the skin, singed the bristles, caught the blood in a dish, roasted the pig basted with its own blood, ate it with his son and wife, and sold the rest. Though the Teacher dwelt at a monastery near by, not once in all those years did Cunda offer him so much as a handful of flowers or a spoonful of rice, nor do any other work of merit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 10 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day a disease attacked him, and while he yet lived the fire of the Great Hell of Avici rose up before his eyes, a consuming torment whose flames shoot a hundred leagues and in which beings burn without being destroyed. His behavior altered with his deeds: crawling on hands and knees from the front of the house to the rear, he grunted and squealed like a pig. His household overpowered and gagged him, but nothing could stop the ripening of his past deeds, so they barricaded the doors and stood guard while he crawled within for seven days. Monks passing heard the squealing and told the Teacher that Cunda had been killing pigs without pity all week. 'He has been killing no pigs,' said the Buddha; 'retribution has overtaken him while still alive; today he died and was reborn in Avici.' The evildoer, be he layman or monk, suffers here and suffers after death, in both places equally.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 10 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Righteous Lay Brother and the Six Chariots

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A righteous householder of Savatthi, father of seven sons and seven daughters, fell dying and begged the monks to recite the Satipatthana Sutta at his bed. Six deities from six heavens came in gleaming chariots to carry him off, and when he cried 'Wait! wait!' his weeping children thought he feared death. He cast a flower-wreath that clung to the chariot from the Tusita heaven, died, and was reborn a god; the heedful rejoice in both worlds.
summary.zh: 舍衛城一位正信居士育有七子七女，一生廣行布施。病重時請比丘誦念處經，六位天神各乘天車自六重天來接。居士喊「等一等」不願中斷聞法，兒女誤以為他懼死而哭。他擲花鬘套住兜率天車，捨報生天。行善者兩世皆歡喜。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: At Savatthi lived five hundred righteous lay brothers, and their head a householder with seven sons and seven daughters, each of whom maintained the ticket-porridges, fast-day foods, rains-residence offerings, and the rest, so that father, mother, and fourteen children kept sixteen forms of alms. Attacked by disease, he sent for eight or sixteen monks and asked them to rehearse the Satipatthana Sutta, 'common to all the Buddhas,' since he was too weak to see them again. As they began, six chariots a hundred and fifty leagues long, drawn by a thousand Sindh horses, came down from the Six Worlds of the Gods, and each deity in turn invited him to his heaven, saying that as a clay vessel is broken and replaced with gold, so beings pass to celestial worlds. 'Wait! wait!' cried the layman, unwilling that the recitation be interrupted; the monks stopped, the children wept that even their father feared death, and the monks, judging it no time to stay, departed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 11 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Recovering himself, the layman told his astonished sons he had been speaking not to the monks but to the six deities, and asked which heaven was most delightful. 'The World of the Tusita gods,' they answered, 'the abode of the mothers and fathers of the Buddhas.' 'Then throw a wreath and say, let it cling to the chariot from Tusita.' The wreath flew and hung suspended in the air from an invisible chariot, and the populace, seeing the garland but not the car, were told, 'I am going to Tusita; if you wish to be reborn with me, do works of merit as I have done.' So saying he died, set foot in the chariot, and was reborn a deity three-quarters of a league tall with sixty cartloads of ornaments and a golden mansion. When the monks told the Teacher they had been stopped, he explained the six chariots and where the man was born: the heedful, laymen or monks, rejoice here and rejoice after death, in both places equally.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 1, story 11 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Little Wayman, the Dullard Who Learned by Rubbing a Cloth
title.zh: 小路尊者——以拭布開悟的愚鈍者

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Little Wayman, born on the road to a runaway bride, entered the Order under his arahant brother but was such a dullard that in four months he could not learn a single stanza, and was expelled. As he set out to become a layman again the Buddha met him, gave him a clean cloth, and told him to rub it saying 'Removal of Impurity'; watching the cloth soil from his own body he grasped impermanence and won arahatship, then multiplied himself a thousandfold before Jivaka's almsgiving.
summary.zh: 私奔少女途中所生的小路，隨證果的兄長出家，卻愚鈍至四個月學不會一偈，被逐出僧團。還俗途中遇佛，受一塊淨布，邊拭邊念「去除垢穢」，見布被己身弄污而悟無常，證阿羅漢並通曉三藏；於耆婆供僧時分身千尊。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: A rich merchant's daughter, shut on the top floor of a seven-storied palace, sinned with her own slave and fled with him; a son was born by the roadside, and a second on the road again, so the boys were called Big Wayman and Little Wayman, 'born on the way.' Their grandfather, the treasurer of Rajagaha, brought up the boys; Big Wayman heard the Buddha preach and became a monk, winning arahatship, and received his little brother into the Order. But Little Wayman was a dullard: in four months he could not learn the single stanza about the lotus and the Buddha resplendent as the sun, for in the dispensation of Kassapa he had mocked a slow-witted monk struggling with the text. His brother told him he could never reach the goal and expelled him; Little Wayman, who loved the religion sincerely, resolved to become a householder rather than leave the Order's gates of his own will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 2, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Jivaka Komarabhacca invited five hundred monks for the morrow and Big Wayman accepted the invitation 'for all except the lay disciple Little Wayman,' the boy concluded his brother's affection was gone and set out at dawn to return to the world. The Buddha met him on the road, took him back as his own pupil, seated him by the Perfumed Chamber, and gave him a perfectly clean cloth: 'Face the east, rub this cloth, and say, Removal of Impurity! Removal of Impurity!' As he rubbed, the cloth grew soiled from his own body, and he thought: this cloth was clean, and by this body of mine it has lost its character. The Teacher, appearing before him in a luminous image, taught that lust, hatred, and delusion, not dirt, are the true impurities to be washed away, and at the stanzas' end Little Wayman attained arahatship with the supernormal powers and mastery of the Three Pitakas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 2, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Jivaka's meal the Teacher covered his bowl and asked whether there were no monks in the monastery; when Big Wayman said there were none, the messenger found the mango-grove full: Little Wayman had filled it with a thousand created monks, some making robes, some repeating the texts. Sent for, a thousand voices cried 'I am Little Wayman!' until the messenger seized the first who said so, whereupon the rest vanished. Then the Teacher told a past life: a devoted but hopeless pupil at Takshashila could learn nothing, so his teacher taught him a single charm, 'You're rubbing! you're rubbing! Why are you rubbing? I know too!' By this charm, repeated at the right moment, he terrified tunnel-thieves and later a barber about to cut the king's windpipe for the commander-in-chief; the king made the dullard commander himself. That pupil was Little Wayman, that teacher the Buddha: refuge given to a dullard ripens, once as worldly wealth and once as the wealth beyond the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 2, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: How Prince Magha Became Sakka, King of the Gods
title.zh: 馬伽太子如何成為帝釋天王

region.en: Vesali; Heaven of the Thirty-three (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 毗舍離；三十三天（象徵性座標）

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Asked by the Licchavi prince Mahali whether he had really seen Sakka, the Buddha told of the human prince Magha, who cleared a road 'treading the Path to Heaven' with thirty-two companions, built a rest-house despite the headman's false accusation, and fulfilled seven vows; by heedfulness he was reborn Sakka, and his merits flowered as the palaces of the gods. His wife Wellborn, who gave nothing, was reborn a crane, learned the precepts from Sakka in fish-form, and after lives as potter's daughter and Asura maiden became his bride, sparing the garuda fledglings by turning back the chariot.
summary.zh: 離車王子摩訶利問佛可曾見帝釋。佛說其前世為馬伽太子，與三十二友修路造屋、力行七誓，因不放逸生為帝釋；其功德感現天宮、善法堂。不曾作福的妻子生為鶴鳥，帝釋教其五戒並化魚試之，歷生陶師之女、阿修羅女，終為天妃，且為不傷金翅鳥雛而回車。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Prince Magha of the village of Macala in Magadha cleared a standing-place for others at the village square, and when he was pushed aside made himself another, until he saw that making room for men was meritorious. He took a spade, cleared a threshing-floor of ground, lit fires in cold weather, and set to smoothing the roads, telling all who asked that he was 'treading the Path to Heaven.' Thirty-two men joined him. The village headman, furious that they refused fish, flesh, and drink, accused them to the king as robbers, and the king ordered them trampled by an elephant; but Magha bade his companions keep hearts full of love for king, headman, and elephant alike, and the beast would not touch them even matted in heavy matting. Pardoned, honored with an elephant and a village, the thirty-three built a rest-house at the crossing of four highways, with chambers for kings, for the poor, and for the sick, thirty-three seats, and a stone seat under an ebony tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 2, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Magha's wife Goodness bribed the builder to carve the pinnacle 'This is the Hall of Goodness,' and let it be bought only for a share in the building; Joy dug a bathing-pool and Thoughtful laid out a flower-garden, but Wellborn only adorned herself. Magha kept his seven vows, supporting parents, honoring elders, speaking gently, shunning backbiting, giving freely, speaking truth, and quelling anger, and dying was reborn Sakka, his companions the gods of the Thirty-three, the builder the god Vissakamma. The Asuras who grew drunk were flung headlong into the ocean, and from the merits of the hall arose the Victory Palace and the Yellowstone Throne, from the tree the Coral-tree, and from Goodness's share the Moot-hall of the gods, whose name men still quote for any charming place. When Wellborn died she was reborn a crane in a mountain cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 2, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sakka carried the crane to heaven so his three wives could mock her ragged beak and legs, then taught her the Five Precepts, warning her to eat only fish that died naturally. Disguised as a dead fish he tested her three times; three times she let the wriggling fish go. Dying, she was reborn a potter's daughter at Benares, to whom Sakka, driving a cart of jewels disguised as cucumbers, gave celestial treasure 'to the woman that keeps the Precepts.' Reborn next as the daughter of the Asura king Vepacitti, she chose as husband the aged Asura in whose form Sakka stood, crying 'He is my husband!' and threw the garland. Sakka flew up crying 'I am Sakka,' and when the Asuras pursued, he bade Matali turn the Victory Chariot back at the cries of the garuda fledglings, who feared being crushed: 'Let not so numerous a host perish because of me alone.' The Asuras, sure he must have reinforcements, fled, and Wellborn became chief of twenty-five million nymphs, for whose sake images of Indra still stand guard at the gates of the City of the Gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 2, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.
